newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arafat briefs Mubarak in Egypt on Hebron talks.
newsitem.headline: Arafat briefs Mubarak in Egypt on Hebron talks.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat briefed Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Sunday about his negotiations with Israel on the West Bank town of Hebron, widely expected to end in agreement within days.
In Jerusalem Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reminded the world a deal on Israeli redeployment in Hebron did not mean Jews would leave the town.
"Anyone who tells you we are leaving Hebron is telling you a lie. We're there and we're there forever. The Jewish people are not leaving Hebron," Netanyahu told American students.

Mubarak and Arafat said nothing to reporters and Arafat left Cairo to return to Gaza. He was to meet Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai later in the day at the crossing between Israel and the Gaza Strip.
Arafat often consults Mubarak at key stages in negotiations with Israel and sometimes asks the Egyptian leader to argue the Palestinian position with the Israelis.
Israeli and PLO officials have said they expect Netanyahu and Arafat to sign an agreement giving the Palestinians control of 80 percent of Hebron by the end of the year.
Hebron is the last of seven West Bank cities Israel agreed to return under an agreement signed in 1995. It occupied the whole West Bank, including East Jerusalem, in 1967.
"We expect an agreement on Hebron to be signed within the next day or two," David Bar Illan, Netanyahu's media adviser, said on Saturday.
U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross is to return to Israel on Monday to mediate any last-minute snags and attend the signing.
Under the deal signed before Netanyahu took office in June, Israel was to have left most of Hebron some 10 months ago.
But Netanyahu delayed implementation, demanding better security for 400 militant Jewish settlers who live among 100,000 Arabs in the city, a flashpoint of violence.
Palestinians had rejected any changes but Bar Illan said "some corrections and changes have been made" to the original agreement. He did not elaborate.

In an apparent gesture of goodwill towards Palestinians, Israel reopened Hebron University on Saturday. The university had been closed last March after a series of Islamic suicide bombings in Israel killed 59 people.
President Mubarak has said a Hebron agreement could clear the way for talks to resume between Israel and Syria after a gap of almost nine months.
But Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara said in Cairo on Sunday one theory about the Hebron talks held that Israel wanted to improve its image.

"The other theory is that after finishing off the question of Hebron, Israel will go into a serious process towards resuming negotiations on all tracks, that is on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks," the minister said after talks with Mubarak.

"Naturally we would welcome that, but on condition that the negotiations resume from the point they reached and that there is a commitment to what was agreed on withdrawal to the border of June 4, 1967," he added.

Syria, in a claim corroborated by Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and some Israelis, says the previous Israeli government said it could eventually return all the Golan Heights, captured in 1967. The Israeli government elected in May does not want to return any part.
